entities.summary: Vettius Valens was a 2nd-century Hellenistic astrologer, a somewhat younger contemporary of Claudius Ptolemy, who made significant contributions to the field of astronomy and astrology. His most notable work, the 'Antiteles', provided a comprehensive system for calculating planetary positions and eclipses. Valens' work was widely used for centuries, influencing the development of Western astrology. The exact date of his birth is unknown, and he died in 175 CE. His legacy can be seen in the continued use of his astronomical tables, which remained in use until the 18th century. The Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus noted Valens' expertise in astronomy, and the Greek historian Eusebius of Caesarea referenced his 'Antiteles' in his own works. Valens' work was also recognized by the Roman Emperor Commodus, who awarded him a grant of land and titles. Despite his significant contributions to the field, the details of Valens' life remain somewhat obscure, reflecting the often-limited record-keeping of ancient historians. In recent years, archaeologists have uncovered a number of Valens' works, including the 'Antiteles', which have shed new light on his life and work.
